Title: Rubikards
Pitch_Text:
Open boosters, build your board, discover community-made illustrations and share your own in Rubikards, a collectible card game blending creativity and idle game mechanics.

Rubikards is a mobile game based on the themes of our school, Rubika, whose game design revolves around incremental gameplay and a strong community-driven aspect, placing content creation and sharing at the heart of the experience.
SumUp_Text:
Rubikards is a project designed to simulate a professional production, in which our school acted as the client. This framework led us to work under constraints similar to those of a real project, especially regarding visual constraints.

This project allowed me to explore advanced topics related to network programming and online data management, while also introducing me to a more structured production pipeline.

Project developed as part of my studies at Rubika Valenciennes.
Realisation_Text:
As a programmer on Rubikards, I handled most of the technical aspects related to the game's core systems and infrastructure. My main contributions were:

• Card architecture: The goal was to design a modular system allowing card characteristics to be defined, such as their effects (handled via IDs), their type (active or passive cards), as well as other community-related parameters. This implementation was particularly challenging since players could create their own cards directly in-game.

• Network programming: Due to the nature of the project, we had to implement an online database system. The goal was to allow players to create and share their cards while voting for their favorites. This required handling player accounts, SQL queries, and online image storage. All of this was implemented through a third-party service: Supabase, used to store cards and community creations.

• Asynchronous programming: Network constraints introduced the issue of latency. Since online servers cannot respond instantly to requests, I used "async" and "await" to prevent blocking the game when performing network operations.

• UI and Input System: This project helped me become familiar with mobile input systems (click, hold, drag, and swipe). I also used this opportunity to work with interfaces, a concept that was new to me at the time. They allowed me to build a highly modular system that required very few changes even after three months of production, which was a first for me.
Amelioration_Text:
One of the main challenges of Rubikards was time estimation for the different tasks. Many of the concepts were completely new to me, and the initial scope felt unrealistic within the given timeframe. However, a clear schedule and a well-managed production made it possible to free up enough time to implement what we initially planned.

This project allowed me to learn many key concepts and to apply them in a concrete production environment.
